The current aim in the development of third-generation steels for light-
weighting automotive applications is to increase strength keeping at least the
same formability as current steel concepts. In this philosophy, an optimal
concept would be one that brings, in addition, a lower density. For this pur-
pose, low-density steels have been designed with important aluminum addi-
tions obtaining density reductions of 8–10% or higher in comparison with low-
carbon steels. At the levels required for lightweighting, aluminum introduces
complex phenomena in steels. Here, some of the effects of aluminum in phase
stability, CALPHAD-type modeling, and microstructure development are
described, the latter in relation with mechanical properties. Finally, the potential
of two families of lightweight steels for automotive applications is assessed by
comparison with a steel currently present in automotive structures.

the application of aluminum even at the small
quantities he recommended (0.1–0.15%). Hadfield’s

Chaˆtelier. The discussion showed that aluminum

for steels. Osmond discussed, probably for the first

ferrite stabilizer by saying, ‘‘If the curve of cooling of

point.’’

INCORPORATING ALUMINUM IN FE-C
THERMODYNAMIC CALCULATIONS
Aluminum as a strong ferrite stabilizer makes
binary Fe-Al alloys basically ferritic, and when ad-
ded in sufficient quantities (Al > 6 wt.%) to low
carbon steels, the matrix will be ferritic. The
simultaneous addition of C and Mn leads to the
presence and stabilization of austenite down to low
temperatures. Aluminum additions bring, besides
order–disorder transformations, another complex
metallurgical phenomenon to steels: spinodal
decomposition. This has been observed in the
quarternary FeMnAlC system,<sup>21,22</sup> but it should
also occur in the ternary FeAlC system.<sup>7</sup>
Another particularity of the addition of high lev-
els of Al is the replacement of cementite by an or-
dered carbide, the j-phase. This phase has a
perovskite structure, designated as E2<sub>1</sub> in the
Strukturbericht classification, but with an uncom-
pleted occupancy of the C atom. The formula com-
monly used is the

even though results
from the literature differ from this formula, mainly
in the case of the ternary system Fe-Al-C and the
relation between Fe and Al. To tailor the micro-
structures and because of the multiple combinations
possible, thermodynamic calculations are required.
This has not been possible until recently because of
the lack of a proper thermodynamic database that
takes into consideration the effect of large additions
of Al.
The incorporation of CALPHAD-type modeling
into the study of phase equilibria in the ternary Fe-
Al-C started with the work of Hari Kumar and
Raghavan.<sup>23</sup>

formalism<sup>24</sup> for the solution phases. Even though
they recognized that the j-phase presents a range of
compositions they used an average fixed composi-
tion of

. They produced a liquidus pro-
jection and eight isothermal sections together with a
complete reaction scheme.

lations into CALPHAD modeling to calculate the
formation energy of the j-phase

ceeded with the CALPHAD approach taking as

interstitial sublattice was used for the description of

structures and the j-phase was modeled with an-
other model also with two substitutional sublattices.
In this case, the j-phase was treated as a solid-
solution phase. Comparing the calculated energies
of formation from the j-phase and the related L1<sub>2</sub>,
they determined that interstitial carbon enhances
the stability of the L1<sub>2</sub> structure. Their thermody-
namic modeling of the Fe-Al-C phase diagram is in
accordance with the experimental work by Palm
and Inden.<sup>11</sup>
Conne´table et al.<sup>26</sup> did not find the thermody-
namic model in Ref. 25 satisfactory and reassessed the
Fe-Al-C system. They proposed a new CALPHAD
description of the j-phase based on their order–
disorder model for the face-centered cubic (fcc)
phase with four substitutional sublattices but re-
stricted the carbon contents to 20 mol.% C. together
with new ab initio calculations, the latter described
elsewhere.<sup>27</sup> The fcc and bcc interactions in the Al-C
system were revised using experimental results
from the ternary system,<sup>11</sup> something that was not
done before. In the Al-Fe system, the fcc description
(c-loop) was improved with the help of an ordering
contribution. These revisions improved the ternary
description of the fcc and bcc phases where they
used the experimental tie lines given in Ref. 11 at
1200C as a guide. The comparison of the modeling
with the experimental isothermal sections was sat-

good. The rather large solubility of carbon in ferrite
shown at 800C and 1000C in Ref. 11 was assumed

probe microanalysis measurements and is not
reproduced by the model. The Al-Fe system was
further revised by Sundman et al.<sup>28</sup> using a four-
sublattice model for the bcc phase (in addition to the
already modeled fcc phase) and using the most re-
cent experimental data.

dered branch of the fcc phase but as a separate

to a binary FeAl lead to complex microstructures

phase equilibria and phase morphologies. Here, a
couple of examples of the relation between micro-

SUMMARY
In this overview, the complexity of introducing
high-aluminum additions has been highlighted from
the point of view of thermodynamics, microstruc-
ture development, and properties. An important
step forward has been taken with the introduction
of high aluminum contents in the frame of CALP-
HAD-type modeling leading to new thermodynamic
databases. The evolution of the microstructure is
complex, but a good understanding has been
reached. It shows that there is still room for
microstructure improvement and better mechanical
properties. In their actual state, the combination of
properties and density reductions in lightweight
alloys shows an important potential for automotive
applications. All this allows proceeding with a
larger risk assessment concerning upstream and
downstream processing for industrial applications.
